identity.title: Beyond Self-Repellent Kernels: History-Driven Target Towards Efficient Nonlinear MCMC on General Graphs

problem.claim: Improve random-walk algorithms on discrete state spaces, including general undirected graphs, for efficient sampling from a target distribution.

gap.claim: Self-repellent random walks incur overhead from computing all-neighbor transition probabilities and are restricted to time-reversible MCMC, limiting compatibility with non-reversible methods.

contributions.claim: Introduces a history-driven target framework that replaces the original target with a history-dependent target based on empirical past visits, rather than directly modifying the transition kernel.
Designs the framework to use only local current/proposed-state information and support both reversible and non-reversible samplers.
Provides a memory-efficient Least Recently Used cache for scaling graph sampling to large general graphs.

stated_novelty.claim: The stated distinction is to drive sampling through a history-dependent target distribution instead of direct transition-kernel modification, while preserving lightweight local implementation and sampler compatibility.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that HDT retains unbiased samples for target distribution μ and near-zero variance performance.
The authors report consistent performance gains in extensive graph-sampling experiments.
The authors report that an LRU cache ensures scalability to large general graphs.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper proposes improving random-walk sampling on discrete spaces such as general graphs.
It situates the problem alongside self-repellent random walks, which use past visit frequencies to prioritize under-sampled states.
It identifies computational overhead and exclusion of non-reversible MCMC as limitations of SRRW.
HDT replaces the original target with a history-dependent target derived from empirical visit history.
The abstract reports local-information implementation, reversible and non-reversible compatibility, retained sampling properties, performance gains, and LRU-based scalability.

source_observation.claim: The abstract explicitly links an implementation choice—history-dependent target substitution—to local-information requirements and compatibility with both reversible and non-reversible samplers.

lessons.interpretation: A method claim becomes more informative when its design mechanism is tied directly to operational and compatibility consequences.
lessons.application: When presenting a new sampling method, state the central design substitution and immediately map it to computational locality and the class of algorithms it supports.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when those consequences are not established by the reported method or when the design has multiple interacting mechanisms that cannot be isolated.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the conditions, guarantees, or evaluation protocol supporting unbiasedness and near-zero variance.
Experiment datasets, baselines, metrics, and quantitative performance gains are not reported.
The mechanism and measured scaling behavior of the LRU cache are unspecified.
